newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 1.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- UNDERWRITING CHANGE FOLLOWS OFT CRITICISM

British merchant banking group Schroders has responded to criticism of City practice by the Office of Fair Trading and moved to introduce a more competitive method of underwriting share issues. The move by Schroders came as part of a 22m stg rights issue by hotels group Stakis and is understood to have saved the group 400,000 stg after part of the underwriting fees were put up for competitive tender. The Schroders innovation comes as City banks and large investment institutions seek to avoid a referral of their system of fixed underwriting fees to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
-- UK SHOWDOWN ON WORKING WEEK

A ruling due from the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in 10 days is expected to force the most bitter row to date between the UK and its European Union partners. The ECJ is expected to implement a maximum 48-hour working week in the UK. However, British ministers, who have resisted the measure since it was contained in a 1993 directive, have threatened to veto any EU reforms at the current intergovernmental conference unless the expected judgement is overturned.
-- EU PENSIONS DEBATE DIVIDES MINISTERS

A report from the Commons all-party social security committee into Europe's public pension schemes has thrown into sharp relief the divisions in the cabinet over Britain's membership of the planned single European currency. The report details the potential negative fiscal consequences of 'unfunded' pensions schemes in other EU countries, and its publication is said to have reopened the rift between Euro-phile chancellor Kenneth Clarke and social security secretary Peter Lilley.
-- BRUSSELS APPROVES FRENCH BUDGET PLAN

The European Commission has defied objections from Britain and Germany by giving approval to a plan by France for reducing its budget deficit to remain on track to qualify for a European single currency. Both the UK and Germany had questioned the legitimacy of the plan, which involves using FFr37.5 billion (4.51 billion stg) of pension fund transfers from state-controlled telecoms operator France Telecom. Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said the decision by the Commission would challenge other countries which seemingly do not meet the Emu criteria to take similar measures.
-- CBI REJECTS LABOUR STAKEHOLDER PLANS

The Confederation of British Industry has rejected Labour party suggestions for German-style two-tier boards for companies in order for economic 'stakeholders', or for opening boardrooms to stakeholders' representatives. The CBI report accepted that there is public concern over the pay of directors and the role of non-executive directors in supervising executive directors, but said that more representation for stakeholders - employees, customers, suppliers - is not the solution.
-- INTEGRATED TELEPHONE SYSTEM DEVELOPED

Scottish-based company Telecom Sciences Corporation (TSC) has developed a low-cost system offering small and home-based businesses the advantages of large, computer-based telephone exchanges. TSC manufactures its Imagination system for the Dutch electronics giant Philips, after buying out Philips' telecoms manufacturing business in Airdrie for 28.1 million stg just nine months ago.
-- BIDDERS SOUGHT FOR DIGITAL TV 'LAND' SERVICES

The UK has become the first country in the world to offer digital terrestrial licenses (DTT) after the industry regulator Independent Television Commission sought applications from operators for four blocks of frequencies (multiplexes). DTT services are capable of offering up to 35 digital television services, broadcast from land-based transmitters on hills and decoded via a 'black box' attached to domestic TV sets.
-- MMC TO PROBE COWIE BUS DEAL

John Taylor, the corporate and consumer affairs minister, has referred the 282 million stg acquisition by Cowie of British Bus to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. Cowie, the motor and finance group, already operates some bus services, and the agreed takeover of privately-owned British Bus was referred because of concern over competition on some services, particularly in south London and the south east.
-- P&U IN SECOND PROFITS WARNING IN THREE WEEKS

Swedish-US pharmaceuticals company Pharmacia & Upjohn has warned that analysts' forecasts for 1997 earnings per share are too high. The caution follows another profits warning just three weeks ago, when the company said that expectations for third quarter results, published on Thursday, were too high. P&U reported third-quarter net profit of $203.7 million, with sales up 2 percent to $1.72 billion. The sluggish sales were boosted somewhat by the launches of two products, Camptostar for bowel cancer, and Xalatan for glaucoma.
-- HUNGARIAN TELECOMS GROUP POISED FOR $500M FLOATATION

The Hungarian national telecoms company, Matav, is to be floated within the next 18 months in an IPO expected to raise about $500 million. The sale of the 16 percent tranche in Matav means that Deutsche Telekom and Ameritech, which own 67 percent of the company, will lower their stake to 51 percent. The Hungarian government currently retains a 25 percent holding in Matav, which was the first east European operator to be privatised, in 1993.
